units: USD. Every rate or percentage is a decimal fraction (0.014 = 1.4%). tableA/tableB rows are [lowerBound, marginalRate]: the rate applies to NJ taxable income (NJ-1040 line 42) above lowerBound, up to the next row's lowerBound. tableASubtract/tableBSubtract give the official shortcut: tax = income x rate - subtract, for the same row. childTaxCredit.table rows are [maxNJTaxableIncome, creditPerChild]: use the first row whose max >= income; above the last row the credit is 0. dependentCareTable rows are [maxNJTaxableIncome, shareOfFederalCredit].

filingThreshold.rule: A resident must file if gross income for the entire year was MORE than the threshold. Someone below it should still file to get back NJ tax withheld or estimates, or to claim the NJEITC or another refundable credit. The 2025 return is due April 15, 2026. A 6-month extension is valid only if at least 80% of the tax (line 45) is paid by the original due date.

exemptions.rules: Line 6 gives $1,000 for yourself, plus $1,000 for your spouse/CU partner on a JOINT return only, or for a registered NJ domestic partner who does not file a NJ return. Line 7 gives $1,000 for each of you who was 65+ on Dec 31. Line 8 gives $1,000 for each of you who was blind or disabled on Dec 31. Line 9 gives $6,000 for each honorably discharged veteran (proof of discharge needed the first time). Line 10 gives $1,500 for each qualified dependent child and line 11 gives $1,500 for each other dependent; both follow federal dependent rules. Line 12 gives an extra $1,000 for each dependent who was under 22, a full-time student at an accredited postsecondary school for at least 5 calendar months, and whose tuition and maintenance you paid at least half of. Part-year residents prorate exemptions by months of residency. NJ has no standard deduction.

2025.wageRules: NJ-1040 line 15 is the total of W-2 box 16 (State wages) from all jobs inside and outside NJ, counting pay in cash, benefits, digital assets or property. NJ wages are often HIGHER than federal box 1. EXCLUDED from NJ wages: employer and employee 401(k) contributions up to the federal limit (not the federal Thrift Savings Plan), qualified commuter transportation benefits up to a limit, and Archer MSA contributions that are excludable federally. INCLUDED in NJ wages (taxable) even when pre-tax federally: (1) contributions to any retirement plan other than a 401(k), such as 403(b), 457(b), 414(h) pension contributions (e.g. NJ PERS/TPAF) and TSP, taxed in the year earned; (2) Section 125 cafeteria-plan salary reductions, meaning pre-tax medical/dental/vision premiums, health FSA and dependent-care FSA (sec. 129), which TB-39(R), TAM 2011-14 and NJ-WT treat as NJ-taxable wages (only a narrow non-salary-reduction 'benefit dollars' plan is excludable); (3) HSA contributions, because NJ does not follow the federal HSA tax breaks. If a taxable cafeteria-plan amount is missing from box 16, the employee must add it back. Tips and overtime are fully taxable: the federal OBBBA tips/overtime/senior deductions do not apply to NJ. Not taxable (not wages): unemployment compensation, NJ temporary disability, Family Leave Insurance benefits, workers' compensation and Social Security. A portal estimator should use box 16. If it starts from gross pay instead, it should subtract only 401(k) deferrals (plus commuter benefits and Archer MSA), not 403(b)/457/414(h)/TSP, Section 125 or HSA amounts.

propertyTax.incomeLimits: There is NO upper income limit. To qualify you must have been domiciled in NJ and kept your principal residence there as a homeowner or tenant, and the home (owned or rented) must have been subject to property taxes. NJ gross income must be more than $20,000 ($10,000 for single or MFS) unless you were 65+, blind or disabled, in which case you can claim the $50 credit even below the threshold. Homeowners count property taxes paid on the principal residence, limited to their ownership share on the deed. Tenants count 18% of rent paid as property tax. MFS spouses who share a home use half of the taxes or rent, with a $7,500 deduction cap or a $25 credit. Part-year residents count only taxes or rent for the months they lived there. You claim ONE of the two benefits: the deduction (line 41, cuts taxable income, up to $15,000) or the refundable $50 credit (line 56). Worksheet H says the deduction is better when it lowers tax by $50 or more ($25 for MFS in the same home).

eitc.rules: NJEITC is 40% of the federal EITC (40% from tax year 2020 onward), refundable, claimed on line 58. You must be a NJ resident who meets the federal EITC rules except the age limits. Filers with no qualifying child can claim it from age 18 with no upper age limit (federally the childless range is 25-64); the credit is figured as if they qualified federally. The taxpayer, spouse and every qualifying child need a valid SSN, so ITIN filers cannot claim it. MFS filers qualify only under the federal separated-spouse rule: a qualifying child lived with you more than half of 2025 and you lived apart from your spouse for the last 6 months. Part-year residents prorate by months of NJ residency. For 2025 the maximum NJEITC runs from $260 (no children) to $3,218 (3+ children). Federal 2025 AGI limits: single/HOH $19,104 / $50,434 / $57,310 / $61,555 and MFJ $26,214 / $57,554 / $64,430 / $68,675 for 0/1/2/3+ children. The investment income limit is $11,950. Refunds that include the NJEITC may take longer because of extra review.

childTaxCredit.rules: Refundable credit (line 65) for each dependent child who is age 5 or younger on the last day of the tax year (under 6). It requires NJ taxable income (line 42) of $80,000 or less, and MFS filers are not eligible. Filers with an SSN or an ITIN can claim it. Part-year residents prorate by months of residency. Households not required to file can claim it through SimpleFile.NJ.gov, launched July 2026 for tax year 2025. These are the same amounts as tax years 2023 and 2024.

2025.dependentCare: The NJ Child and Dependent Care Credit (line 64, Worksheet J, attach federal Form 2441) is a percentage of the federal child and dependent care credit you were allowed, based on NJ taxable income: up to $30,000 = 50%; over $30,000 to $60,000 = 40%; over $60,000 to $90,000 = 30%; over $90,000 to $120,000 = 20%; over $120,000 to $150,000 = 10%; over $150,000 = no credit. It has been refundable since tax year 2021. You must be allowed the federal credit, and MFS filers qualify only under the federal exceptions. Civil union couples who do not file jointly at the federal level redo the federal credit as if married filing jointly.
2025.retirementExclusion: Pension exclusion (line 28a): you or your spouse/CU partner must be 62+ or disabled (Social Security definition) on Dec 31, and NJ total income (line 27) must be $150,000 or less. With total income up to $100,000, exclude up to $100,000 (MFJ), $75,000 (single/HOH/QW) or $50,000 (MFS) of taxable pensions, annuities and IRA withdrawals. From $100,001 to $125,000, exclude 50% (MFJ), 37.5% (single/HOH/QW) or 25% (MFS) of that income. From $125,001 to $150,000, exclude 25%, 18.75% or 12.5%. Above $150,000 there is no exclusion. Other retirement income exclusion (line 28b): if you are 62+ with income of $150,000 or less, and wages, business, partnership and S-corp income total $3,000 or less, any unused pension exclusion can be applied to other income. A special exclusion of $6,000 (MFJ/HOH/QW) or $3,000 (single/MFS) applies if you cannot receive Social Security or Railroad Retirement benefits. Social Security, Railroad Retirement and US military pensions are fully exempt.
2025.otherStateCredit: Claimed on Schedule NJ-COJ (line 44), with a separate schedule for each jurisdiction or each tax. Credit = the LESSER of (a) income tax actually paid to the other jurisdiction, or (b) NJ tax x [income taxed by both NJ and the other jurisdiction / NJ gross income (line 29)]. The ratio is carried to 7 decimals. The NJ tax used is the tax on line 39 minus the property tax deduction, worked in columns for the deduction and the credit cases. The credit can never exceed the NJ tax on line 43. No credit is allowed for tax paid to the US government, Puerto Rico or any foreign country or territory. For a NJ resident working in New York, the 'income taxed by both' must be the 'New York State amount' actually taxed on NY Form IT-203. Under the NJ-PA Reciprocal Agreement, Pennsylvania does not tax a NJ resident's compensation, so those wages are taxed only by NJ and need no credit. The agreement does not cover Philadelphia or other PA local wage taxes, and those qualify for the credit: eligible income = Philadelphia wage tax withheld / the nonresident rate (2025: 3.44% from Jan to Jun, 3.43% from Jul to Dec).
2025.sharedResponsibility: Still in force: NJ Health Insurance Market Preservation Act, P.L.2018, c.31, effective from tax year 2019. Residents who must file, and everyone in their tax household, need minimum essential coverage all year or an exemption; otherwise they pay the Shared Responsibility Payment on line 53c. You are automatically exempt if not required to file, i.e. line 29 is $20,000 or less ($10,000 for single/MFS). The amount follows IRC 5000A as in effect on 12/15/2017 but uses the NJ average bronze premium. It is the greater of a flat amount ($695 per adult, $347.50 per child, $2,085 maximum) or 2.5% of household income above the filing threshold, prorated for months without coverage. It is capped at the statewide average annual bronze-plan premium. The Division's 2025 range is $695 to $4,908 for an individual, with a family maximum of $24,540 (household income of $400,001 or more). Exemptions are claimed on Schedule NJ-HCC. They include coverage costing more than 8.05% of household income, income at or below 138% of the federal poverty level, a gap of less than 3 consecutive months, religious sect or health-care sharing ministry, tribe membership, incarceration, living abroad and hardships (F-1 to F-12). Filers can also ask for help from Get Covered New Jersey (line 53b).
notes: Tax computation: if NJ taxable income is under $100,000 you may use the official Tax Table, which comes in income bands and can differ from the schedule by a few dollars. At $100,000 or more you must use the rate schedules. The shortcut is tax = income x rate - subtraction amount from the matching row.
Quirk: the official Table B row for $70,000 to $80,000 subtracts $1,154.50. A strict bracket-by-bracket calculation gives $1,155.00, so the official schedule is $0.50 higher in that band.

NJ gross income (line 29) is the sum of separate income categories: wages, interest, dividends, business profits, net gains, pensions/IRAs, partnership share, S-corp share, rents/royalties, gambling, alimony and other income, minus the retirement exclusions. It does not start from federal AGI. A net loss in one category counts as zero and cannot offset another category, except through the ABC adjustment.

Interest: interest on bonds of OTHER states and their localities (out-of-state municipal bonds) is taxable (line 16a). Interest and gains on NJ state/local obligations and on direct US obligations (Treasuries, savings bonds) are exempt, as is the exempt part of a distribution from a NJ qualified investment fund.

Capital gains (line 19, Schedule NJ-DOP) are taxed at the same rates as other income; there is no lower capital-gains rate. Losses cannot be carried back or forward, and there is no active/passive distinction.

Medical expenses (line 31): unreimbursed medical costs for you, your spouse and your dependents above 2% of NJ gross income (line 29), plus qualified Archer MSA contributions and self-employed health insurance (limited to earned income). Insurance premiums count as medical expenses. HSA contributions are not deductible.

ABC adjustment (line 35, Schedule NJ-BUS-2): for tax years 2016 to 2025 you subtract 50% of the 'business increment', which is regular business income minus alternative business income (it lets losses in one business category offset others). See the 2026 tiers.

College Affordability deductions (lines 37a-c), allowed only if NJ gross income is $200,000 or less: NJBEST 529 contributions up to $10,000, NJCLASS loan payments up to $2,500, and tuition at a NJ college up to $10,000.

Use tax (line 51) is 6.625% of taxable purchases made without NJ sales tax, or taxed below 6.625% (online, mail-order, out of state); see Worksheet K. Without records you can use the Division's chart based on NJ gross income: up to $15,000 = $14; $15,001-30,000 = $44; $30,001-50,000 = $64; $50,001-75,000 = $84; $75,001-100,000 = $106; $100,001-150,000 = $134; $150,001-200,000 = $170; over $200,000 = about 0.0852% of income, up to $494.

Excess employee payroll contributions (lines 59-61, only when you had more than one employer): the 2025 employee maximums were UI/WF/SWF $184.02, DI $380.42 and FLI $545.82. Anything withheld above these becomes a refundable credit.
Other credits not modeled: sheltered workshop (46), Gold Star Family counseling (47), employer of organ/bone-marrow donor (48), Wounded Warrior caregivers (62), pass-through BAIT credit (63).
Civil union partners use the same filing statuses as spouses, so the NJ status can differ from the federal one.

The Division's 'Income Tax Changes for Tax Year 2025' page lists no rate, exemption or credit changes. The CTC stays at the doubled 2023 level, the NJEITC stays at 40% and the CDCC percentages are unchanged. NJ Direct File is not available because the IRS ended Direct File.

2026.changedFrom2025: Changes enacted for tax year 2026: (1) NJ Child Tax Credit up 25% for tax years 2026-2028 (P.L.2026, c.26, S4531, approved June 30, 2026): $1,250 / $1,000 / $750 / $500 / $250, with the same $80,000 cap, under-6 age rule and no MFS. The 2025 amounts return for 2029 and later. (2) ABC adjustment now depends on gross income (P.L.2026, c.22, A5323, approved June 30, 2026, retroactive to Jan 1, 2026): 50% of the business increment if NJ gross income is $500,000 or less; 25% if over $500,000 up to $1,000,000; nothing over $1,000,000. (3) New exclusion for gains on qualified small business stock when the gain is also excluded federally under IRC 1202 (P.L.2025, c.67, A4455, for tax years starting on or after Jan 1, 2026). I found NO change to rates or brackets, filing thresholds, exemptions, the property tax deduction or credit, the NJEITC percentage, the CDCC percentages, the retirement exclusions, the medical floor or the Shared Responsibility Payment law. The FY2027 budget summaries (Governor, NJBIA, NJCPA, EY, CBIZ, Sax) report no rate change. The Division has not yet published the 2026 NJ-1040 or its instructions. Its rate page (updated Sept 28, 2026) still calls the current schedule '2020 and After'.

filingThreshold.rule: Unchanged from 2025: you must file if gross income for the year was more than the threshold. The 2026 return will be due April 15, 2027.

exemptions.rules: Unchanged from 2025 (same rules); no 2026 amendment was found.

2026.wageRules: Same as 2025. Line 15 = W-2 box 16. Only 401(k) deferrals up to the federal limit, commuter benefits and Archer MSA contributions are excluded. 403(b), 457, 414(h), TSP, Section 125 cafeteria-plan salary reductions (health premiums, FSA, DCAP) and HSA contributions all stay in NJ wages. A bill to give HSAs the federal tax treatment (A2634, 2026-27 session) was only introduced, not enacted. Tips and overtime stay taxable, since NJ does not follow the federal OBBBA deductions for 2025-2028.

propertyTax.incomeLimits: Same as 2025: no upper income limit. NJ gross income must be over $20,000 ($10,000 for single/MFS), unless you are 65+, blind or disabled, who can still get the credit. The FY2027 budget changed only the separate Stay NJ / ANCHOR rebate programs, not the NJ-1040 deduction or credit.

eitc.rules: Same rules as 2025: 40% of the federal EITC, refundable, age 18+ with no upper limit for filers without children, SSN required (no ITIN), and prorated for part-year residents. The 2026 dollar amounts follow the IRS's inflation-adjusted 2026 federal EITC tables. Bills to raise the credit to 45% or open it to ITIN filers (S3797, S2198) had only been introduced as of the last check.

childTaxCredit.rules: From P.L.2026, c.26 (S4531), for tax years 2026, 2027 and 2028. The credit is per child who has not reached age 6, so age 5 or younger at year end. It requires NJ taxable income of $80,000 or less and is not available to MFS filers. SSN or ITIN filers can claim it. It is refundable and prorated by months of residency.

2026.dependentCare: Same NJ percentages as 2025: 50% / 40% / 30% / 20% / 10% of the federal credit for NJ taxable income up to $30k / $60k / $90k / $120k / $150k, and nothing above $150,000; refundable. NJ law sets the credit as a percentage of the federal credit allowed for that tax year. The federal credit itself rises from 2026 under OBBBA (higher federal credit rate), so the NJ credit should rise too. This last point is my own inference; the Division has not issued 2026 guidance.
2026.retirementExclusion: Unchanged from 2025: age 62+ or disabled, NJ total income $150,000 or less. Up to $100,000 (MFJ) / $75,000 (single/HOH/QW) / $50,000 (MFS) when income is $100,000 or less. 50% / 37.5% / 25% of the income from $100,001 to $125,000. 25% / 18.75% / 12.5% from $125,001 to $150,000. The other-retirement-income and special ($6,000/$3,000) exclusions are the same. The Division's page was updated 9/28/2026 with no changes.
2026.otherStateCredit: Same as 2025: Schedule NJ-COJ, credit = lesser of tax paid elsewhere or NJ tax x (income taxed by both / NJ gross income), never more than the NJ tax. The PA reciprocal agreement still applies.
2026.sharedResponsibility: Still in force for 2026. The Division's calculator offers a 2026 SRP estimate, and no repeal was found. The formula is the same as 2025 (greater of $695 per adult / $347.50 per child, $2,085 maximum, or 2.5% of household income above the filing threshold, capped at the NJ average bronze premium). The 2026 bronze-premium cap had not been published on the Division's SRP page as of Oct 2026.
notes: ABC adjustment for tax year 2026 and later (P.L.2026, c.22): 50% of the business increment if NJ gross income is $500,000 or less; 25% if over $500,000 up to $1,000,000; 0% over $1,000,000.

QSBS: starting with tax years that begin on or after Jan 1, 2026, gains on qualified small business stock are excluded from NJ gross income to the extent IRC 1202 excludes them federally (P.L.2025, c.67).
Estimated payment due dates for 2026: April 15, 2026; June 15, 2026; September 15, 2026; January 15, 2027.
Federal OBBBA deductions (tips, overtime, seniors, car-loan interest, SALT changes) still do not affect the NJ return for 2025-2028 (Division OBBBA page).

Everything else (capital gains at ordinary rates, out-of-state bond interest taxable, 2% medical floor, $10,000/$2,500/$10,000 College Affordability deductions under $200,000 gross income, use tax at 6.625%) is unchanged, with no 2026 amendment found.

SimpleFile.NJ.gov (Code for America with the Division) lets people who are not required to file claim the CTC. The Governor's July 10, 2026 release says the credit rises from up to $1,000 to up to $1,250.

refundStatusDetails: The online 'Where Is My Refund?' tool is at https://www20.state.nj.us/TYTR_TGI_INQ/jsp/prompt.jsp. The automated phone line is 1-800-323-4400 (24/7). Expect at least 4 weeks after e-filing, at least 12 weeks after mailing, and 15+ weeks for returns needing extra processing or paper returns sent by certified mail (Division page, updated 1/28/2026). Returns claiming the NJEITC may take longer.
freeFiling: The Division's own 'NJ Online Income Tax Filing' at https://www.njportal.com/Taxation/NJ1040/ is 'a free service for New Jersey residents who do not wish to use paid services'. It handles resident NJ-1040 returns only, and you must have filed a NJ return for the prior year and confirm it with that year's gross income. It currently files tax year 2025, with 2022-2024 also selectable, and has fewer features than paid software. A nonresident version is at https://www.njportal.com/Taxation/NJ1040NR/. 'NJ Direct File' is closed and not available for tax year 2025 because the IRS ended Direct File. Free in-person help: IRS VITA for low/moderate income, people with disabilities and limited-English speakers (1-800-906-9887), and AARP Tax-Aide/TCE mainly for ages 60+ (1-888-227-7669). Households that are not required to file and want only the NJ Child Tax Credit can use SimpleFile.NJ.gov.
estimatedPayments: You must make estimated payments (Form NJ-1040-ES or online) if you expect to owe more than $400 after withholding and credits. Due dates are April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15 of the next year, moved to the next business day after a weekend or holiday (2025 Q2 was June 16). Underpayment interest (Form NJ-2210) is charged only on the shortfall below the lesser of 80% of current-year tax (two-thirds for qualified farmers) or 100% of prior-year tax, and the prior year must have been a full 12-month return. Other exceptions: tax on prior-year income at current rates and exemptions, annualized income, or 90% of tax on actual income for each period. The rate is prime + 3%, charged only up to April 15. Note: N.J.S.A. 54A:9-6(d)(3) sets a 110% prior-year safe harbor when NJ gross income is over $150,000 ($75,000 MFS). However, the Division's notice says it computes interest only against 100% of last year's tax or 80% of this year's, and GIT-8 (Jan 2026) and NJ-2210 (2025) show only the 100% rule.
nonresident: Form NJ-1040NR is for nonresidents with NJ-source income whose gross income from everywhere for the whole year is over $10,000 (single/MFS) or $20,000 (MFJ/HOH/QW), or who want a refund of NJ withholding or estimates. There is no part-year return. A part-year resident files NJ-1040 for the resident months and also NJ-1040NR if they had NJ-source income while a nonresident. Exemptions, deductions, credits and retirement exclusions are prorated by months. Pennsylvania residents who work in NJ fall under the NJ-PA reciprocal agreement for wages (see the NJ-1040NR instructions).
unverified: 2026 rates, brackets, filing thresholds and exemptions are marked 'unchanged' because no enacted change was found and the Division still labels its schedule '2020 and After' (page updated 9/28/2026). The 2026 NJ-1040 and instructions are not published yet.

The 2026 NJ Child and Dependent Care Credit increase is my inference: NJ's percentage applies to the federal credit allowed, and OBBBA raises the federal credit from 2026. The Division has not confirmed this.

HSA treatment: no current Division publication says it directly. The basis is the A2634 (2026) bill statement ('the tax advantages provided under federal law are not available under the current New Jersey gross income tax'), TB-39(R) and TAM 2011-14 on cafeteria plans, NJ-WT, and secondary sources (Newfront, Cooper Levenson).

Whether Section 125 health premiums (already taxed as NJ wages) can be counted in the NJ medical-expense deduction is an inference. The Division allows insurance premiums as medical expenses but I found no explicit statement about cafeteria-plan premiums.

The Shared Responsibility Payment bronze-premium cap for 2026 is not published. The flat amounts ($695 / $347.50 / $2,085) and the 2.5% rate come from the 2018 OLS fiscal estimate and IRC 5000A as of 12/15/2017, matched against the Division's 2025 $695 minimum. The Division's own pages show only the ranges.
Use tax chart, top row: the Division page text reads '0852% (.00852) of income, or $494'. Continuity with the $170 row implies 0.0852% (0.000852); treat the exact factor as unconfirmed.

Estimated tax 110% rule: the statute and an old Division notice mention it for income over $150,000, but the current GIT-8 and NJ-2210 use 100% of prior-year tax. The estimator should use the 100%/80% test.
NJEITC 2026 stays at 40%. The pending bills S3797 (45% plus ITIN) and S2198 (ITIN) were last seen 'introduced' on a third-party tracker that may lag behind the legislature.
I could not confirm what information the refund-status tool asks for (for example the exact refund amount), because I did not open or use the tool.

Bill status and P.L. chapter numbers for S4531 (c.26), A5323 (c.22) and A4455 (P.L.2025 c.67) were checked on LegiScan and confirmed against the enacted-law texts on pub.njleg.gov. The 2025 per-line instruction PDFs used are on njportal.com, the Division's filing site (public PDFs only, no login).
